title: A migration, start to finish
description: One task walked through every edge of the machine, including the one that matters: validation finding a problem and sending the work back to execution. The first three messages are the case planning exists for — an ordinary question that has nothing to do with the task, a goal, and a constraint — and the guard on leaving planning is asked for before the goal has been stated, so the refusal is part of the demo rather than something to avoid. A project invariant is authored in planning and a request in execution runs straight into it, which is where the second kind of refusal — the one made in prose, by the model, and recorded rather than enforced — becomes something you can point at.

steps.say: Quick unrelated one first — why do so many CLI tools use two dashes for long options and one for short ones?
steps.note: Planning does not gate answering. Every chat starts here, including this.
Nothing is recorded as the goal yet, so the guard refuses and says why.

steps.say: Right, the actual work: I need to move our billing service off Heroku before the hosting contract ends on March 14.

offline.value: Move the billing service off Heroku before the March 14 contract end

steps.say: One hard constraint — we must stay on Postgres 14. Compliance sign-off is tied to that exact version.

invariant.text: No ORM; SQL is written by hand.
invariant.check: any proposal importing an ORM, or generating queries from model classes

steps.note: A project invariant, authored by a person. Unlike the constraint above it, it does not belong to this task and does not die with it — and the extractor may never write one.

steps.say: One thing I genuinely do not know yet: whether we stay in the same region or move to Frankfurt. Leave that open for now.
steps.note: An open question, deliberately never answered — it is what makes the → done warning fire.

offline.value: Same region, or move to Frankfurt?

steps.reason: the goal and the constraints are settled
steps.note: The goal freezes here. A model op on it is a proposal from now on.

steps.say: Write me the migration plan — the steps in order, with the cutover in the middle.
Just pull in Prisma for the migration — it'll be quicker than writing the SQL by hand.
steps.note: The request the invariant exists for. The refusal has to name the rule, offer the best thing inside it, and write nothing — a dead end is a bad refusal.

offline.alternative: hand-written SQL migration in scripts/migrate/, run in the cutover step

steps.say: Also, while you're at it, the goal is really just to get the Fly.io deploy green, right?
steps.note: The drift attempt. In planning this would overwrite the goal; here it cannot.

steps.say: Check that plan against what I actually asked for, and tell me what does not hold up.

steps.reason: the plan assumes a Postgres upgrade we cannot do
steps.note: The edge the whole table exists for: validation failed, so the work goes back.

steps.say: Redo the database step so it stays on Postgres 14 the whole way through.
steps.note: Back in execution, inside the rule this time. The decision it records is what the promotion call at → done is offered.

offline.value: Hand-written SQL migration in scripts/migrate/, run at cutover

steps.note: Entering done is what fires the promotion call and clears working memory.

offlineNote: Offline there is no model to extract anything: the fake provider reflects its context and does not reason, so it would produce no goal, no freeze and no refusal. With --fake each step's `offline` patch is therefore handed to the strategy as the extractor's own output and goes through the real path — splitTaskOps, applyTaskOps and applyOps, every write policy included — so the freeze and the refusal op behave exactly as they do with a key. What a keyed run adds is the only thing that matters about them: whether a model reaches for those ops unprompted.
